item.title: When Weight Loss Meds Flatten More Than Appetite
item.description:
Emotions

When Weight Loss Meds Flatten More Than Appetite

Patients taking GLP-1 medications can experience emotional blunting.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 medications have many positive health benefits.
  • Some people experience the unpleasant "Meh effect."
  • This effect is likely due to changes in the neurotransmitter dopamine.

One of my favorite movies of all time is Annie Hall, starring the late, great Diane Keaton. However, the original name of Woody Allen’s classic was “Anhedonia.” The studios didn't think that title was marketable because it means the inability to feel pleasure. Probably not the best choice for a rom-com.

Since the explosion in GLP-1 prescribing, I am hearing from more of my patients who take this class of drugs that they feel “Meh.” They are clear to point out that they are not depressed and do not feel sad or hopeless. Instead, they tell me they'd rather sit on the couch and watch Netflix than go to the gym or do any previously pleasurable activities. It's not quite depression. It's not exactly fatigue. Instead, it's a feeling of emotional flatness—a sense that life has lost some of its “color.” The foods they once loved no longer excite them. Shopping feels unnecessary. Hobbies become less engaging. Even celebrations can seem muted. Patients often describe themselves as emotionally "neutral," "disconnected," or simply "blah."

Sometimes referred to as the “Ozempic personality,” these feelings are thought to be related to changes in the brain’s reward center. The brain chemical most commonly affected appears to be dopamine, the neurotransmitter associated with motivation and reward. A positive effect of GLP-1 medicines is that they effectively quiet the “food noise” that individuals who are overweight struggle with. They have also been shown to decrease cravings for substances other than food, such as alcohol and nicotine. A 2022 review of the medical literature found that GLP-1 drugs resulted in “potent reductions in alcohol and substance abuse.”

This effect is not limited to humans. Several years ago, Professor Anders Fink-Jensen traveled to the island of St Kitts to investigate heavy drinking among its inhabitants. The inhabitants he studied were not human—the Velvet monkeys that live on the island are apparently notorious for sipping on cocktails stolen from visiting vacationers. Dr. Jensen provided unlimited quantities of alcohol to a group of monkeys who were pretreated with Ozempic. Significantly, those monkeys drank far less than their untreated counterparts.

Not everyone who takes a GLP-1 medication will experience this effect. Some actually feel better emotionally because of increased energy, less joint pain, improved sleep, and overall increased confidence. It is not clear why some individuals experience the GLP-1 "meh" effect. Probably it is due to a combination of genes, brain chemistry, and underlying mental health conditions. The “meh” effect is not depression, and I warn my patients who are starting these medications not to feel they are having a relapse of a mood disorder as they express thoughts like “nothing feels exciting,” “I don't feel joyful,” or I feel flat.”

Some people find new sources of pleasure outside of food. For example, after losing weight, you can take up exercise in some form, walk with friends, or start a new hobby like gardening, painting, reading, or traveling.

How To Manage The GLP-1 “Meh Effect”

  • Remember to eat a healthy diet even though you will feel full sooner. Eating less can impact your brain. Without its usual supply of nutrients, you may feel more foggy, have difficulty concentrating, or forget more often.
  • Exercise. Your body does not selectively lose fat. When you are taking a GLP medication, you will also lose muscle mass. Offset this by engaging in resistance or weight training. Any kind of exercise is good for brain health, and it can positively affect your mood and motivation.
  • Sleep well: lack of sleep harms brain health. Aim for 7-8 hours per night, and stay off your screens for at least 60 minutes before bed. Your brain is like a computer—it has to shut down in stages.
  • Stay hydrated: Drink enough water. The goal is 64 ounces per day. Dehydration can add to fatigue and a flat feeling.
  • If you have reached your goal weight, talk to your doctor about possibly lowering your GLP dose. It has been shown to improve the “meh.”

GLP-1 medications are transforming the treatment of obesity and other chronic illnesses. They improve metabolic health, decrease the risk of obstructive sleep apnea, and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. However, every medication, even aspirin, has effects beyond its primary target. While evidence suggests GLP-1 receptor agonists influence the brain's reward pathways, it is still unclear whether emotional blunting—or the so-called "meh" effect—is a direct medication effect, an indirect consequence of changes in food reward, or a combination of biological and psychological factors.

Providers should recognize that patients' emotional experiences are as important as the numbers on the scale. The ultimate goal of treatment is not simply weight loss—it is improved overall health, well-being, and quality of life.

item.title: Anger, Laziness, and the Roots of Procrastination
item.description:
Procrastination

Anger, Laziness, and the Roots of Procrastination

Why do we procrastinate and how can we quit doing it?

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • It is human nature to procrastinate.
  • Procrastination has a purpose in humans and other creatures.
  • Procrastination is a choice, whether conscious or unconscious.
Sisyphus by Titian
Source: Wikimedia Commons

Why do we procrastinate on doing tasks or engaging in various other activities in life? This is a frequent question many people bring to psychotherapy.

What is Procrastination?

Intellectually, rationally, they know they "should" do what needs to be done--whether washing the dishes, doing homework, paying bills, visiting an old friend, washing and sorting clothes, working out at the gym, maintaining the house or car, filing taxes, starting to date again, going to the dentist, etc, etc.--and recognize that it is not rational or practical to avoid doing so, but, for some mysterious reason, simply cannot bring themselves to face the music, so to speak, which, in the case of procrastination, is usually experienced as unpleasant or annoying.

We tell ourselves and others that we want and intend to take care of the task or situation, but then we don't do anything. It can be a disconcerting experience and distressing realization: We are not the master in our own metaphorical house but, rather, we are a house divided. We are not fully in control of ourselves. We are not the one calling the shots. We are not of one mind. There are unknown (unconscious) forces at work within us that oppose our conscious will.

Our rational goals are derailed by something irrational within us. Being confronted with this disturbing and disquieting fact of life--for if we are not calling the shots, making the decisions, then who or what is, and what might that eventually lead to?--can be deflating but, it is also the beginning of wisdom.

Why We Procrastinate

What causes us to delay or avoid doing certain things? Things which we feel we want or need to or should be doing? Perhaps a more helpful question to begin with would be: What motivates us to do what we do everyday?

There are tasks and activities that most of us do daily. For example, getting out of bed in the morning, making the bed, brushing our teeth, showering, shaving, dressing, eating breakfast, going to work or school, etc. Why do we do these things? Partly, because they are habitual and have become our daily routine because we consider them necessary and essential.

At some, typically unconscious, level, we do these tedious tasks every morning because we were as children trained to do so by our parents or caretakers, sometimes under threat of punishment if we refused. And, at a more adult level, we accept that these behaviors are expected of us by our parents, spouses, and society and are required to participate and co-exist in the the world with others.

Yet, there are those that, for different reasons, refuse to participate in such daily rituals. Some, like the so-called puer aeternus or puella aeterna, are psychologically stuck in childhood or adolescence and do not feel the necessity of or responsibility for committing to attending to such mundane, ordinary details of life.

But most often, this is due to some emotional or psychological state such as profound depression, severe substance abuse, or psychosis. Such severely afflicted individuals have lost their motivation, see no need to perform these mundane daily tasks, and frequently refuse to do so.

They no longer seem to care about taking care of themselves or living up to any of society's expectations of them and, in some cases, either do not have the energy to perform these rituals regularly or are rebelling consciously or unconsciously against doing them.

These people or patients are typically very angry in general--with their parents, other authority figures, with life or fate, and with themselves--but direct their rage at rejecting and rebelling against society and its rules, regulations, expectations, norms, etc. (See my prior post.) When taken to an extreme, this negative and hostile attitude toward the world can devolve into nihilism, psychopathy, and violence. (See Diamond, 2022.) But, fortunately for civilization, much more often, this anger or resentment takes the passive form of procrastination.

Is Procrastination a Kind of Laziness?

Are we who procrastinate simply lazy? Just not interested enough in such things to expend sufficient time or energy to do them? Laziness is a universal trait in human beings, animals, insects, and other creatures. We tend to think of laziness as a negative quality and lazy as a pejorative term, but it is only nature: the organism needs time to rest, relax, and just be.

In the case of non-human creatures, choosing not to pursue prey or other food sources that are not worth the effort or trouble is a way of conserving energy for use in more essential activities. The same is true with humans. Laziness is an archetypal or existential aspect of our creatureliness or primitive animal nature, concerned primarily with not wasting time or energy on non-essential activities, seeking pleasure, and, whenever possible, avoiding pain or discomfort. So, yes, we are all lazy, like dogs, cats, lizards, etc. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but, if taken too far, can contribute to our proclivity for procrastination.

We all procrastinate at times, but some make a habit or way of life of it. Chronic procrastination can cause what French existential philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre (1953) called a state of mauvaise foi or being in "bad faith" with oneself, an inner lack of integrity and authenticity, a sense of existential guilt and feelings of anger with oneself for avoiding reality or being too lazy.

Procrastination and the False Sense of an Eternal Present

Psychiatrist and holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl recognized that, existentially-speaking, we cannot as adults allow ourselves the luxury of procrastination. A future is not guaranteed to anyone. This is one of the distressing existential facts of life. Death is an ever-present possibility, an eventual inevitability. In a sense, to procrastinate is to unconsciously deny or diminish the existential fact of death.

Indeed, procrastination is a pervasive expression of what Ernest Becker (1973) called "the denial of death." And by denying or not acknowledging the ever-present possibility and eventual inevitability of death, we provide ourselves with the perfect opportunity and create a convenient excuse for more procrastination. Why not? We have all the time in the world. There's no hurry. The dishes will still be in the sink tomorrow. The laundry can wait. So, why bother with it today? It's not important. I'll get to it later.

While there is some truth to this way of thinking and we definitely do need to prioritize how and when to expend our limited precious time and energy, procrastination, like any other avoidant behavior, can become a bad habit or compulsive addiction. Constantly distracting ourselves with new, exciting, and challenging activities instead of facing the tedious, unglamorous, and dirty tasks of existence can become a way of life. We avoid doing things that make us feel anxious, resentful, or bored, begin to feel anxious, guilty, or annoyed with ourselves for procrastinating, and then procrastinate some more in an attempt to avoid these uncomfortable feelings, ad nauseum.

In this way, procrastination becomes a vicious cycle that is, much like other avoidant behaviors, bad habits, and addictions, difficult--but certainly not impossible--to break.

item.title: Why Do We Hold Our Opinions So Tightly?
item.description:
Identity

Why Do We Hold Our Opinions So Tightly?

What we believe may be less revealing than why we need to believe it.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • An opinion becomes harder to revise when changing it feels like changing who we are.
  • Before defending an opinion, ask what being wrong would mean about you.
  • Some opinions do more than express what we think; they also signal where we stand.
  • Strong conviction is not the same thing as strong evidence.

During a conversation at dinner last week, I felt my chest tighten, heat rise in my body, and my jaw clench. Someone said something I disagreed with. But before I had chance to think anything through, the words fell from my mouth, “No, that’s not right.”

The physical reaction came first. The reasons for my disagreement came afterwards.

What struck me was how quickly I became agitated and felt the need to disagree.

When a Preference Becomes an Opinion

If I were to say, “I love heavy metal,” this is a preference. It cannot be disproved because it is simply a description of my subjective experience. However, if I change that slightly to, “heavy metal is the best genre of popular music,” I have shifted from the subjective to the apparently objective. I am no longer telling you what I like; I am making a statement about how things are. And crucially, I have turned you into someone who either agrees with me, or is wrong.

For the purposes of a thought experiment, it might be useful to distinguish between three kinds of statement:

  • Preference: “I love heavy metal.” This is purely a report on my subjective experience.
  • Opinion: “Heavy metal is the best form of music.” This presents an evaluation as though it describes something about the world.
  • Testable claim: “Heavy-metal musicians demonstrate greater technical ability on X measure.” Now we have specified something that evidence could potentially support or contradict.

What fascinates me about the opinion category is that it can sound like a factual claim without necessarily giving us an agreed way of deciding who or what is right.

This raises the question: Why does being right matter?

What Is an Opinion Actually For?

Psychologists have traditionally studied attitudes rather than opinions as such. For our purposes, an opinion could be thought of as an internal evaluation that is often expressed explicitly.

Katz (1960) suggested that attitudes can serve different psychological functions, including helping to organise our experience, express values, and maintain aspects of our self-concept. Shavitt (1990) later provided experimental evidence that attitudes towards different things can serve a variety of functions related to social identity and self-esteem.

This is interesting because we might think that an attitude is simply the end result of our reasoning: I considered the evidence and reached a conclusion. However, Functional Attitude Theory suggests that attitudes can also serve psychological functions for us.

This shifts the question from “Why do I believe this?” towards “What does believing this say about me?" Does it allow me to express a value, maintain my self-image, feel part of a group, or make sense of a confusing world?

One interesting clue comes from research in which people were asked factual questions about politically charged issues. When Bullock and colleagues offered small financial rewards for accurate answers, the gap between opposing groups became considerably smaller. This suggested that at least some of the original disagreement wasn’t simply about what they believed to be true; it was also influenced by their allegiance to a particular side. In other words, what I say may reflect something about where I stand as well as what I know.

But belonging may only be part of the story. Sometimes a position can be tied up with something more personal: who I understand myself to be.

What Happens When an Opinion Becomes Me?

We might think that strongly held moral positions are primarily about social belonging: the idea that “these are the views my people hold.” However, across three studies, Novak and Skitka (2025) found that stronger moral conviction was consistently associated with the extent to which people felt an attitude expressed their personal identity, rather than simply their membership of a particular group.

What’s interesting is that if my opinion has become evidence of who I am — good, intelligent, informed, sophisticated, compassionate, responsible — then revising that opinion may carry an entirely different psychological cost. It may require me to rethink something about how I understand myself.

Why Does Disagreement Feel So Personal?

Which brings me back to what happened at my dinner table.

If you were to pause a moment and reflect, what happens in your body when someone challenges an opinion you hold strongly? Do you become curious, or do you notice tightening, heat, urgency, irritation, or an immediate urge to correct them?

And then the important question:

At that point, am I still curious about what the other person is saying, or am I already defending my position?

The reaction itself doesn’t tell you why you're responding this way. But it does tell you there may be something worth paying attention to. Why do I need to be right? What would being wrong mean? What would changing my position cost me? What am I actually defending here — a position based on evidence, a preference, a value, an affiliation, or an identity — or several at once?

Coming back to my music analogy, imagine I say that “heavy metal is the most sophisticated form of popular music,” and someone replies, “Well, heavy metal is just noise.” If my opinion is connected to how I see myself, their response may feel like a challenge to my intelligence, taste, and identity.

Can You Hold Your Opinions More Lightly?

This might provide an opportunity to revisit the idea of preference. Sometimes changing the language might reveal what we’re actually trying to say.

“This is how I see it.”
“My preference is…”
“My current view is…”
“The evidence I've seen leads me to think…”

Those phrases don't weaken my position; they simply acknowledge that this is my perspective rather than an absolute fact.

If you’d like to try this as an exercise, you could notice a strongly held opinion, then see if you can move it in one of two directions.

1. Can I acknowledge the subjectivity in it?

“Actually, I simply prefer this.”

2. Or can I turn it into something testable?

“What exactly am I claiming, what evidence supports it, and what evidence would persuade me to revise it?”

If I can’t do either, that's when things get interesting.

The deeper question becomes: Why do I need to hold this opinion so tightly? Who would I be if I allowed myself to see things from a different perspective?

Perhaps the challenge isn't to stop having opinions but to hold them lightly enough that they remain ideas we have rather than identities we must defend. There may be considerable freedom in moving occasionally from “This is how it is” towards “This is how I currently see it.”
